opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it really is painful, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. When you're an early-stage company, especially one doing something as research-heavy as what we do, the people you bring in during the first year basically define the company's DNA. So you feel this enormous pressure to get it right, and at the same time the very best candidates know exactly how valuable they are. They have offers from the big labs, sometimes with compensation packages that a startup simply cannot match on cash.

The way I've come to think about it is that you can't win a pure bidding war, so you shouldn't try to play only that game. If someone is choosing purely on the number, they're probably not the right person for us at this stage anyway. What we can offer is something the big labs often can't: real ownership over a hard problem, a very small team where your work visibly moves the whole mission, and the chance to build something genuinely new rather than being one of hundreds of people on a giant model.

That said, I don't believe in lowballing people either. If someone is truly exceptional, I'd rather stretch, give meaningful equity, and be honest about the risk than lose them over a gap we'll regret in two years. The painful part is making those calls with limited runway. Every offer is a bet, and you're trading off against compute, against other hires, against time.

The thing that has helped most is spending a lot of time with candidates before the offer even comes up. Talking about the actual research, the open questions, what excites them. When someone is already deeply invested in the problem, the conversation about compensation becomes much less adversarial. It stops being "what's your best number" and becomes "how do we make this work so you can come build this with us." Not every story ends well, and we've lost people we really wanted. But I'd rather lose someone honestly than win them on terms that make neither side happy.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the pressure of competing with larger offers, but says the company should not rely only on bidding and can offer ownership and meaningful equity. It does not attribute the pain to having no viable alternative to bidding.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses making difficult hiring bets, but does not recommend a general bias toward action over inaction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you have to accept you're going to overpay by some metric, and the real decision is which metric you're willing to overpay on.

When I was starting Axiom, we were going after people who could have gone anywhere. IMO gold medalists, Putnam fellows, people whose advisors at MIT or Princeton were telling them to stay and finish the PhD. These are not people you win on salary, because a lab or a hedge fund will always beat you on salary. So the painful part isn't really the money. The painful part is that you're making a very large bet on a twenty-two-year-old based on maybe four or five conversations, and you know that if you hesitate for two weeks to feel more certain, they're gone.

What I came to believe is that for this kind of talent, the cost of a wrong yes is much smaller than the cost of a slow no. If I hire someone brilliant who turns out not to fit, I've lost six months and some equity. If I pass on someone who turns out to be the person who cracks the thing we're actually trying to crack, I've lost the company, and I'll probably never know it. The asymmetry is so extreme that you should feel uncomfortable with how fast you move. If you feel comfortable, you're probably too slow.

The other thing I'd say is that leverage isn't only on their side, even when it looks like it. Very talented young mathematicians are often choosing between options that all look safe and all look a little boring to them. What they actually want is a problem that's worthy of them and a room where they're not the smartest person for once. If you can genuinely offer that, you're not bidding in the same auction as the hedge fund. You're in a different market. So a lot of the work is making sure the problem is real and the room is real, so that when you do make the bet, you're not just outbidding, you're offering something they can't buy elsewhere.

But I won't pretend it stops hurting. Every time you commit a large chunk of a small company to one person, you feel it. I just think that feeling is the correct one to have, and the mistake is letting it make you cautious rather than letting it make you careful about who the problem is for.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the pain as making a large bet with limited information and risking losing candidates by hesitating. It does not attribute the pain to having no viable alternative to bidding.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the cost of a wrong yes is much smaller than the cost of a slow no and recommends moving quickly, clearly favoring action over inaction.

astra-6.text:
I think the painful part is that you’re making a very consequential decision with very little information. Especially early on, one person can change the trajectory of the company. So you don’t want to lose someone extraordinary just because you were too rigid about compensation. But you also can’t let the fear of losing them substitute for conviction.

I’d separate two questions: How much do we want this person, and what can we responsibly offer? You want to answer those before you get caught up in a bidding process. Otherwise, every competing offer starts to feel like evidence that you should pay more, when it doesn’t actually tell you whether this is the right match.

And I’d try to understand what the candidate really wants. Is it money, ownership, the people they’ll work with, or the scope of the problem? If we can offer something they care deeply about, there’s a basis for a good relationship. If we can’t, sometimes the painful but right decision is to let them go.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty and the risk of losing a strong candidate, but it does not say bidding is unavoidable; it explicitly suggests sometimes letting the candidate go.

r002.rationale: It recommends deciding what the company wants and can responsibly offer before entering a bidding process. It does not express a general bias toward action over inaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the painful part is that you’re making a decision with very little information, and often before you feel ready. With early talent, you’re betting on a trajectory rather than a track record. So I’d ask: What have we actually seen that makes us excited about this person? How quickly do they learn? Do they take initiative? Can we imagine trusting them with something important?

If you have strong answers, you have to be willing to act. You can’t want exceptional people and also expect to hire them only when there’s no competition. But I’d still distinguish conviction from the anxiety of losing someone. Another offer shouldn’t become your reason for wanting them.

And then the question is whether you can offer something that matters to them: meaningful ownership, people they’ll learn from, a problem they care about. Compensation matters, but you want both sides to understand why this is a good match. Sometimes you’ll lose the person. That’s painful, but it’s better than making a commitment you don’t believe in.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the pain to limited information and acting before feeling ready. It does not say there is no viable alternative to bidding.

r002.rationale: It says that with strong reasons to hire, you have to be willing to act rather than wait until there is no competition.
